alternative: Use the JVM GC for memory: kotlin.io.use / Closeable for deterministic release of external resources, java.lang.ref (WeakReference, WeakHashMap, Cleaner) for non-owning edges and cleanup backstops, and explicit ownership documented per API - a hand-written owning wrapper cannot control reclamation on the JVM.
idiom_name: none - JVM reachability owns memory; use{} + java.lang.ref at the resource edge
implementation_notes: Kotlin runs on the JVM's reachability-based collector and adds no ownership types, so a class wrapping a heap object with copy/destroy semantics cannot govern when that object dies; what the ecosystem provides is scope-bound release, not ownership. The inline stdlib extension use (with AutoCloseable overloads) runs a block on a Closeable and closes it on every exit path, attaching a close failure as suppressed when the block also throws; java.lang.ref supplies WeakReference/WeakHashMap for non-owning edges and Cleaner for post-mortem release. The classic structure survives only as a wrapper around an external resource, and there use{} or an explicit close() already covers it.
pitfalls: use is an extension on a non-null receiver: a nullable resource needs ?.use { } or an explicit branch, and silently skipping cleanup through a null receiver is a classic mistake.

Coroutine-held resources are not Closeable: tie teardown to structured concurrency (coroutineScope plus invokeOnCompletion/awaitClose) or a try/finally inside the coroutine, not to a scope function outside it.
WeakHashMap holds values strongly while their keys live; caching a value weakly needs a different structure (or java.lang.ref), not a WeakHashMap alone.
Kotlin/Native has its own memory manager and no JVM reference types; do not carry JVM ownership assumptions across targets.
